hints: Look closely at the starting ketone, pentan-3-one, and notice its symmetry on both sides of the C=O group.
Remember that cyanide, $CN^-$, is a strong nucleophile that attacks the slightly positive carbonyl carbon, so think about what type of addition this is.
Trace what happens after attack to the C-O bond, and think about why pure HCN alone is too slow without extra $CN^-$ to start the cycle.
walkthrough:
**Draw the product**

Great start, let's see what we make. The C=O becomes C(OH)(CN).

Chemical equation:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{HCN} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C(OH)(CN)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$

**Check for chirality**

A chiral centre needs four different groups. Here the central carbon is joined to $\text{OH}$, $\text{CN}$, and two identical $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ groups, so it is not chiral.

**Recall the mechanism type**

This is the classic nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl. The nucleophile $CN^-$ attacks the $\delta+$ carbonyl carbon to give an alkoxide intermediate:
$$\text{C=O} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{C(CN)-O}^-$$

**Finish the mechanism and spot the catalyst**

The $\text{C-O}^-$ intermediate then takes $\text{H}^+$ from HCN to give the $\text{C-OH}$ product and regenerate $CN^-$:
$$\text{C(CN)-O}^- + \text{HCN} \rightarrow \text{C(CN)-OH} + \text{CN}^-$$
Because $CN^-$ is reformed, only a small amount (from KCN or NaCN) is needed as a catalyst, and pure HCN alone reacts far too slowly.

options.A: Incorrect. The product is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C(OH)(CN)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The new carbon has two identical ethyl groups, so it has only three different types of group and is achiral. Students often assume every cyanohydrin is chiral, but symmetry here prevents it.
options.B: Incorrect. Addition of HCN to carbonyls is nucleophilic addition, not electrophilic addition. The $CN^-$ ion acts as a nucleophile donating a pair of electrons to the $\delta+$ carbonyl carbon.
options.C: Incorrect. The intermediate after $CN^-$ attack is an alkoxide ion, $\text{C(CN)-O}^-$, not $\text{C-OH}$. The $\text{OH}$ group only forms in the final protonation step when the intermediate reacts with HCN.
options.D: Correct. HCN is a weak acid and provides very little $CN^-$ on its own, so a small amount of $CN^-$ (as NaCN or KCN) is added as a catalyst. It attacks first and is regenerated when the alkoxide intermediate deprotonates HCN.
